item.title: The largest family separation in history
item.description: On farms, billions of mothers and their young can never be together.
item.content:encoded:
Remember the outcry over American influencer Sam Jones, when she posted a video of herself taking a baby wombat from its distressed mother on the side of an Australian road?

40.000 people signed a petition to ask for Jones’ deporation from Australia. The separation of mother and child apparently struck a cord.

At least when it’s about wombats. When it’s about farmed animals, not so much. On Mother’s Day, let’s spare a thought for the non-human mothers - and their children.

The hens who’ll never know their chicks

You know where eggs come from. But have you ever thought about where the chickens who lay the eggs, come from?

They obviously come from other chickens, but these so-called parental animals are even more invisible than the egg-laying hens or the chickens raised for meat.

Parental animals live on what we call breeding farms or parent stock farms, in intensive conditions (nine birds per square meter in the EU). About 10% of the animals in any group are roosters, who have to make sure the fertilisation rate is as high as possible.

These roosters are much larger than the hens, and the latter have no choice but to endure the roosters. Severe injuries from the males’ spurs and claws to the hens’ backs, necks, and wings are common and can be fatal. Even a small bleeding wound can trigger pecking by other chickens, often resulting in death.

When after 70 weeks, the hens’ egg production starts to decline, the hens and roosters are sent to the slaughterhouse. By then, the hens have laid around 170 eggs. These eggs go to a hatchery to be hatched. The female chicks will go to a laying barn as laying hens, and the male chicks are killed on the day they are born.

Born without a mother

Something else most people never think about: when both the egg-laying hens and the broiler chickens peck through their eggshell and see the light, there will be no one around to guide them or give them love. Broilers will be killed after six weeks, without ever having known maternal care.

In “normal” circumstances, a hen already communicates with her chicks while they are still inside the egg. Hens are very protective of both their eggs and chicks, defending them with their life if they have to. Mother hens teach their chicks everything they need to survive, from scratching and searching for food, to finding a safe place to sleep, as well as social behavior.

Chickens who grow up without a mother often imprint on each other, rather than on an adult animal, which can lead to very problematic behavior. Without a mother to model foraging, pecking can turn on other birds - feather and toe pecking may escalate to cannibalism and death. Without a protective adult, birds are also more fearful; so-called “panic crowding” can lead to smothering.

Breaking the bond

I suspect that most people in the meat industry - and many people who eat meat - will dismiss talk of mothers and children, of family bonds and separation, as mere sentimentality.

But motherhood is not a sentimental add-on: it is a hard-won evolutionary adaptation that dramatically boosts offspring survival through protection, nourishment, and the transfer of learned behaviour.

All this, the intensive animal industry destroys - ruthlessly, across all species. A dairy cow is impregnated, gives birth, has her calf taken within hours. She was tricked into producing milk for a calf she will never raise - year after year, until she is worn out. A sow in a gestation crate can feed her piglets through bars, but cannot turn to reach them. And then there are the mothers who never get that far. A British abattoir vet has testified to seeing unborn calves kicking inside the wombs of cows hanging on the slaughter line, bleeding to death.

The tiny Australian wombat had a mother to be taken from. That is why we noticed. The billions of mothers in the animal industry have their children taken before they can even meet them.

For the animal mothers, it’s never a Happy Mother’s Day.

item.title: Benjamin Lay was a vegan, abolitionist dwarf in the 18th century
item.description: Benjamin Lay was a hunchbacked dwarf of four feet tall. He was also a vegan, feminist, and anti-slavery activist.
item.content:encoded:
Benjamin Lay was a hunchbacked dwarf of four feet tall. He was also a vegan, feminist, and anti-slavery activist.

I recently read his biography - The Fearless Benjamin Lay by Marcus Rediker1 - and have wanted to write about him ever since. In our darker moments as animal advocates, when we despair about the gigantic challenges in front of us, it can be helpful to look at how others fought the odds and never gave up.

A radical dwarf

Benjamin Lay was born in England in 1682. He worked as a sailor, a glove maker, and a shepherd. He became a Quaker and married Sarah, who was, just like him, a little person. In the late 1710’s, they went to Barbados together to work as merchants, but were transformed by seeing the evils of slavery (most people on the island were enslaved). Eventually the couple settled outside Philadelphia, and Benjamin spent all his remaining years trying to change what they had witnessed.

He boycotted products from slavery, and fought for abolition for forty years, against the active hostility of his own religious community. The last third of his life, he lived in a cave, next to which he grew his own food in a small garden, made his own clothes from flax because he refused to wear wool, and would not eat any animal flesh at all.

Empathy for little people comes naturally to me. Being only 166 cm (5’5), I know how stature (or lack thereof) can shape how others perceive you (look up heightism). Lay had it far worse. In his own time he was treated as defective. Historians called him “the little hunchback.” His enemies called him deformed in body and mind. In his book, Marcus Rediker argues that being treated as less than human gave Benjamin a moral imagination many of his contemporaries lacked. He knew what it was to be looked through, and carried that knowledge outward, to everyone else he saw being looked through, including animals.

By Rediker’s account, Lay was not a pragmatic or likable activist: he was aggressive, awkward, self-righteous and stubborn. Indeed, he appears to have been a quite obnoxious fellow - possibly a terrible vegan advocate - so we shouldn’t idealize him. But there sure are things to admire in him.

Fellow creatures

This little person mainly fought his own people: the community of Quakers. He challenged them about the fact that in spite of their lofty religious ideals, many of them were slaveholders or were otherwise benefitting from slavery. These were the people he prayed with, the ones who sat beside him in his meeting houses. He was telling those he loved that they were monstrous.

Before Lay became a vegetarian, he killed a groundhog that kept ravaging his vegetable patch, nailing parts of the animal to the four corners of the garden. Not soon after, he regretted what he had done and renounced eating animals. He came to see the connection between the exploitation of humans and non-humans, whom he all called “fellow creatures.” To make clear the connectedness, he quoted Pythagoras:

“As long as Man continues to be the ruthless destroyer of lower living beings, he will never know health or peace. For as long as men massacre animals, they will kill each other. Indeed, he who sows the seed of murder and pain cannot reap joy and love.”

We may not live to see the fruits of our work

Lay fought his various fights for many years, but did not live to see much result. People, including the Quakers, generally didn’t take kindly to his activism. Many said he made slave keeping “too great a sin.” At one point he was physically removed from Quaker meetings (which presumably was not a hard thing to do). He was jailed on occasion. His own Philadelphia Yearly Meeting of Quakers and several other groups ended up disowning him.

Lay died in 1759. The Quakers did not formally prohibit slaveholding among their members until 1776 - which still made them ahead of the rest of the world by a long time (the United States abolished slavery in 1865).

There was a bit of light right near the end of his life, though. A friend brought Lay the news that the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting had finally begun to discipline slave-trading Quakers - which apparently had Lay declare that he could die in peace.

Only in 2017, more than 250 years after his death, the Quakers had the good sense to formally reinstate the man. As of today, most haven’t heard of him.

Animals are still locked up by the billions. Most of the people we love still eat them. Like Benjamin Lay, vegans and animal advocates are considered “too censorious” at the dinner table. Like Benjamin Lay, we may expect (still for quite some time) to be ridiculed, fought and antagonized.

Lay was probably a pretty bad animal advocate, and we shouldn’t copy his self-righteousness. But we can be inspired by the stamina of this small, unusual person - who saw early, alone, and was right.

item.title: The team is bigger than the label
item.description: Gaz Oakley is no longer vegan. That doesn't mean he's no longer an ally.
item.content:encoded:
I’m always interested to see the vegan community’s response when a vegan celebrity jumps ship.

That happened, as you may have seen, with Gaz Oakley, a celebrated Welsh chef and cookbook author, who - as Avant-Garde Vegan - built up a following of two million people. He’d recently shifted to a quieter, rural life, growing his own vegetables and keeping rescued chickens. On a podcast, he said he no longer considers himself vegan, and focuses more on localism, foraging, rewilding etc. He even said he’s open to eating invasive species (crayfish, venison, pigeon…).

Many vegans, of course, have expressed disappointment, anger and frustration with Oakley. They talk and write about a betrayal of values or financial gain. I understand this disappointment, and I do think what Oakley did - and still might do - can cause some real PR damage. I don’t agree with the man’s reasoning about nature (nothing is as clichéd as “reconnecting with nature”) or his aggressive stance on invasive species. I could write a long post on all of this, but others have done so (see e.g. here and here). In this piece, allow me to bring some other thoughts that may be a bit less obvious.

Can we be more charitable?

First of all, as some of my readers will know, I’m in favor of what I call slow opinion. We don’t know everything there is to know about this person, we can’t look in his head, we shouldn’t make assumptions too quickly - definitely not negative ones. Let’s leave some room for doubt.

And let’s try to be charitable. The guy did a lot. He inspired millions to eat more plant-based. There are no doubt people who attribute their going vegan or getting active to Oakley (and those people don’t need to follow him where he went now). Also, he apparently plans to remain mostly plant-based, and is potentially still an ally against factory farming.

In terms of harm, our diets are on a spectrum

Oakley is eating eggs from rescued hens. These products are not without issues (the rescued animals are breeds that are inherently problematic), but we should be able to distinguish lesser harms from bigger harms. Considering all animal products as the same evil doesn’t help anyone. I haven’t found anything about how Oakley would source his fish or his “invasive species”, but in case they would come from hunting, this is - as much as I despise hunting and think it’s wrong - less horrible than an animal spending their entire life in a dark, overcrowded shed.

The same goes for the amount of animal products one consumes: none is great, but less is better than a lot. We can’t pretend someone is going full omnivore again when they say they’re going to eat a few animal products now and then (I’ve seen vegan influencers being totally lambasted for saying they’ll eat this or that product-with-some-animal ingredients on occasion).

Let’s also consider that vegan diets are never entirely harmless, with some products negatively impacting the environment, human labor, or even animals. Oakley may be avoiding some issues that many vegans aren’t.

What if vegans are not the best advocates?

This is a point I’ll explore in another post, but for now: what if vegans are putting the bar too high for the average person, and say 90%-vegans are more convincing or inspiring? I can imagine many more people being attracted to a lifestyle or diet that allows for at least exceptions, than to one that is absolute (no matter how many times we may want to say that animal rights are non-negotiable). As much as we dislike it, dropping the vegan identity may also be helpful in this respect.

Health worries should be taken seriously

Oakley spoke about health challenges. Even though some commenters are skeptical this was the case (saying he only offered those after a lot of backlash), we can’t look into his head (see first point). All I know is that health issues are often a cause for people to abandon ship. It’s not necessarily that their diet is the cause of their symptoms, but it’s understandable that after a long quest trying to get better - and surrounded by pro-meat propaganda in a carnistic environment - they might at least think: “what if…” and maybe experiment.

Pushing him away is not going to get him closer (duh)

The so-called black sheep effect is at work here: defectors from a shared norm will be treated more harshly than outsiders who never signed up. Ex-vegans will incur more ire than meat eaters. With their behavior, the defector may imply that the standard is unlivable or false. That’s very threatening to the ingroup, and it’s part of the reason for the backlash. So after the person left, we bolt the door behind them.

Vegans mocking, criticizing, accusing the man of all kinds of nasty things is a reliable way to drive him even further away. Someone pushed out by their fellow progressives may find a warmer reception elsewhere. The right, in particular, is good at welcoming people the left has shamed - offering them community and a sense of vindication. It’s not what we want.

Let’s look at ourselves

Oakley said he didn’t feel at home in the vegan community. We can ignore that, or take that seriously. There are good reasons to do the latter, because many people feel it - including me at times. We define things very strictly - who is in and who is out, what is right and what is wrong. That is not appealing to many people.

So there’s an irony here: the sort of pile-on against Oakley for leaving may be exactly why he no longer felt at home in the first place. The angrier we are at him, the more we prove his point.

Still on our side?

I had ended my first version of this article like this: Let’s be more forgiving toward those who fall off the wagon, and help them back on.

But that’s actually not the message I want to bring. It would imply the only solution is to get Oakley back at 100% vegan.

What if - as long as he remains largely plant-based, against factory farming, and continues to care about animals - we simply consider him to be on our wagon still?

That would be the kind of inclusiveness that makes our movement larger, our rules less absolute, our appeal wider, and our minds less rigid. And that is, I think, what ultimately helps animals most.

item.title: A small, unforgiving club won't get us there
item.description: On ex-vegans and bigger tents
item.content:encoded:
Renctly I suggested that vegans behave charitably towards Gaz Oakley, the ex-vegan celebrity, and still consider him part of the team that can help animals - at least as long as he’s not going back to being a full-fledged meat eater, speaks up against factory farming, and remains largely plant-based.

First of all, if ex-vegans spout misinformation in public, or turn vehemently against veganism, we are right to explain our point of view and give counterarguments. I wouldn’t be surprised if part of the ex-vegan stories are amplified - sometimes even invented - by pro-meat campaigners. And if an ex-vegan (or anyone) becomes a die-hard carnivore influencer, I don’t think I mind much that they are mobbed and shamed.

Celebrities are a special case, and many people love to hate them. In this article, I make abstraction of Gaz Oakley and other celebrities and influencers, and merely look at how our movement sometimes deals with ex-vegans in general. I’m talking about people who, for sincere reasons, stop being vegan (and don’t brag about it). Celebrities or not, they are often treated quite harshley.

Black sheep effect

Part of what explains this, like I wrote in my previous article, is the black sheep effect: someone who defects from a norm/leaves a group is treated much more negatively than someone who never followed the norm or was never part of the group in the first place.

I understand that. I’m often disappointed when I hear about ex-vegans. Like other commenters, my first reaction may be: you knew everything, you knew about the problems with animal products, you knew how to replace them, you’ve done it for years… and now you turn your back to it all? How could you? And also: you were one of us, and you left us.

Out of this disappointment comes anger. Outrage even. I’ve seen many vegans making comparisons with child molestation, murder, racism etc. They’re using language that (I hope) they wouldn’t use towards their non vegan parents, children, spouses or friends. It’s thwarted expectations (among other things) that make us do this. Note that something like the reverse is also true: we’re all the happier if a person from whom we didn’t really expect it, has a change of heart. How happy we are with the stories of animal farmers turning vegan!

We need to realize that while understandable, this behavior (anchored in evolutionary psychology) is not entirely rational and that it doesn’t help us, nor the animals. How we behave towards the black sheep is important for our movement in several ways.

There are still more ex-vegans than vegans

I wrote about vegans falling off the wagon before. There are more ex-vegans than vegans (same for vegetarians). Many people seem to have problems continuing a vegan lifestyle. Now the reaction of many (present) vegans is interesting: these people were never vegan in the first place, they didn’t do it for the animals, they saw it as a diet…

That’s clearly not always the case. There are people who go vegan for the animals and then give up. We can then say they were never vegan at all, believe that are hypocrites or driven by profit… but how does it help us or the animals if we don’t take ex-vegans seriously?

I don’t find being vegan in this world hard, but I’m surrounded by vegans and animal people, I can find and afford all the plant-based products I want. I don’t have kids or a spouse who want to eat animal products… But for other people, taking into account all the pro-meat advertisements that are being thrown at them, and all the pro-meat nutritional information… I don’t doubt that it can be hard at times to keep it up.

Giving ex-vegans the cold shoulder will make things worse

Imagine a vegan who is struggling. There’s a lot of pressure from the outside. There may be health issues they are dealing with. Maybe their “faith” is wavering. Who can these people turn to? Will they be able to find support, or will they be wary of telling anyone about their doubts, then perhaps fail, and fall off the wagon?

Another problem is this: anyone who sees how ex-vegans are sometimes punished might become less likely to ever go vegan in the first place. We obviously need it to be more normal, fashionable even, to not eat animal products. There are probably quite a few celebrities around (artists, politicians, public intellectuals) who haven’t outed themselves as animal-friendly, or vegan/vegan curious. But if they’ve ever seen the treatment of ex-vegans, their reasoning might be: if I ever have to turn back, for whatever reason, I’ll be destroyed. So either I won’t go vegan, or, if I do, I’ll never say so in public. This would be a shame.

More generally, when we’re posting our reactions and criticisms, we should think about who else is watching. Around every public shaming there can be many people who are silently checking what is going on. What if the lesson they take from this spectacle is not “I should be more committed” but “these are not my people”? While we think we’re punishing a defector, we’re showing anyone still on the fence what awaits them if they ever fall short.

Finally, even people who self-identify as vegan but who, because of criticism from their own side, might choose to no longer do so. Again, that won’t help normalize being vegan.

Tackling the biggest challenge in the world

At the heart of these issues lies how our pro-animal ideology, our compassion, our anti-speciesism often translates to a pretty much all-or-nothing normative behavior. If you’re pro-animal, you should not consume any animal products (otherwise you’re not pro-animal).

Given how little success we are having in convincing people to go vegan (including the fact that so many people can’t even *stay* vegan), this is clearly not the ideal strategy for success. If we treat anyone who’s not aligning their behavior a 100% with the vegan ideal as not part of our team, we are bound to remain a very small club (and we make it very easy to fall off the wagon).

A very small club will not be able to tackle the biggest challenge in the world: to change the diet of eight billion people. So we have to be able to work together with all kinds of people who don’t think exactly the same as us, who make mistakes, who backtrack, who sometimes say the wrong things even. We should be charitable towards them - not just because that shows the compassion we want other people to show towards animals, but also because it’s what’s better for animals. So who is on “the team”? Everyone who intentionally or not contributes to a better situation for the animals on this planet.

In case a black-and-white ideology prevents us from seeing things like this, and keeps insisting that murder is murder and that eating animals is the same as child abuse, we need to remember that there are very different social norms at work in these different spheres. Eating meat is not just acceptable but actively celebrated by 95% of the population, while child abuse is illegal. While what is generally thought does not equal what is actually right, we need to accept that these different norms mean people have different ideas of wrong-doing in these various cases. For most people it’s hard to consider something as wrong when 95% of the people are participating in it.

This understanding alone can help us create a bigger tent - something which I remain convinced is the number one thing our movement needs to do in the years and decades to come.

item.title: No, farmers don't know their animals best
item.description: They're too biased to understand what animals need
item.content:encoded:
Ever had farmers or other animal industry people comment on your social media posts about animal welfare?

Almost invariably, they’ll say you don’t understand the first thing about animals. They are - they claim - the experts on cows and pigs and chickens, and you are at best uninformed, at worst a liar.

Before anything else, let me note that these days, the easiest, laziest but also most popular defense against inconvenient truths is saying that they are lies. People may tell you that you’re lying without anything to back it up. They may put those damn laugh-emojis under your Facebook posts without really knowing why. And their calling you stupid and ignorant may be just… because that’s exactly what they are (oh yes, it can be infuriating).

But other than that, no, most farmers and industry people are not the experts on farmed animals and their welfare. Below is why.

Vegans aren’t perfect (duh)

A concession first. Not wanting to exploit animals does not equal understanding them. A vegan doesn’t necessarily know what an animal wants. Lack of knowledge about animals can lead to wrong conclusions. On occasion, things might be less bad for an animal than an unaware vegan believes (think, for instance, about cows who may prefer their stable over the meadow, in certain temperatures).

Our sympathy for and identification with animals may also lead us to ascribe qualities or feelings to them that they do not have (anthropomorphism).(1)

Vegans and animal people may also idealize animals, believing they’re always the kind creatures of our picture books. But non-humans can at times demonstrate nasty behavior - to humans or to other animals (not that this justifies any mean behavior on the farmer’s part, of course).

Farmers are undereducated about animal welfare

Are farmers in a better position to know what animals want and how they feel?

Working on a farm and being with animals will certainly teach a farmer a thing or two about animals. However, the first thing to remember is that most farmers will never see their animals in a natural environment where they can demonstrate their natural behavior. Experiencing animals only in industrial settings, the farmer is getting a limited view of the animals’ faculties. Perhaps it’s people working on sanctuaries who understand farmed animals best?

And it’s not that the farmers acquire a lot of theoretical knowledge during their studies, which are mainly about getting a profit out of the animals and fattening them as efficiently as possible. The little they learn about animal welfare is taught in function of husbandry, economics, biosecurity or compliance with existing laws.

This is quite a painful gap, when you look at it. Vets, zookeepers, shelter operators and other handlers of animals need to have at least some schooling to make sure they relate to their animals appropriately. But farmers, who may work with up to many thousands of animals and are the main agents contributing to their welfare, graduate without knowing much about animal welfare at all.

Farmers don’t do much better than the general population

For what they’re worth, two data points about farmers’ knowledge about animal welfare.

In the Netherlands, Dr. Leonie Cornips developed a cow language quiz, recording and translating twelve different cow sounds. Over three hundred farmers and more than a thousand members of the public took part, trying to identify what the cow was trying to say from sound alone. While farmers did better than the public, a mere 32% recognized the sound of fear or stress. Nearly half failed to recognize the call of a cow wanting to be milked. The heart-rending sound of a mother crying for her calf was correctly identified by only 31% of farmers, while 45% interpreted it as a positive signal.

Another, older study showed that farmers (called “caretakers” in the study) did not do significantly better at recognizing pig vocalizations than “naive students”, and they did worse than ethologists. Farmers also tended to downplay the emotional intensity of the animals’ cries (e.g. at castration). The researchers hypothesize that “caretakers might use a psychological defense to protect them from feeling intense emotions for the large numbers of animals to which they provide care.”(2)

Biased against seeing animals as beings with interests

The latter, of course, is a major issue. Farmers need to see their animals as products before anything else. Often this conditioning started early, when a farmer was raised on a family farm. Even more so than the rest of us, they learn that animals are there for us to use. If you think of someone as a product, many questions around animal welfare are unlikely to ever arise.

Farmers can’t be the experts on what animals need or how they feel, because there is too much working against them being that. The farmer’s stake in the whole story is even bigger than that of the consumer, because animals are their source of income. As Upton Sinclair wrote, it is hard to make a person understand something if their livelihood depends on them not understanding it.

Biased animal welfare scientists

If you want to learn about animal welfare, the farmers should obviously not be your first resource. But animal welfare science might not be either. It’s not just the industry itself that suffers from structural blinders: the very science used to evaluate animal welfare is often compromised by what some researchers have called “pragmatism bias”.

A 2026 paper published in Frontiers in Animal Science highlights how funding pressures and operational constraints systematically skew scientific inquiry toward short-term gains, symptoms rather than root causes, and intensive production systems. Instead of investigating what animals genuinely need to thrive under ideal conditions, animal welfare science frequently limits its focus to what is economically viable within current industry models.

This creates a closed epistemic loop: by restricting research to incremental adjustments within flawed systems, science inadvertently helps normalize and entrench those very systems, leaving policymakers and the public with a very incomplete view of what animal well-being actually means.

The need to push back

Vegans shouldn’t be too arrogant to say that they know all there is to know about animal welfare, and should be aware of their biases. But even more important is to bring to the fore the biases of farmers and animal welfare scientists working for the industry, and push back against the idea that they are the ones who know animals best.

They don’t.

What they may know best is how to raise an animal most profitably.

Subscribe for more posts that confront, comfort or inspire.

(1) I wrote about anthropomorphism and anthropodenial here.
(2) The industry language of “units”, “livestock”, “yield” or “harvesting” obviously contributes to this defense.

item.title: "Hello, how do you feel about humans exploiting other animals?"
item.description: About a year ago, in June 2025, I had a long discussion with Anonymous for the Voiceless (AV) founder Paul Bashir, on David Ramms’ YouTube channel.
item.content:encoded:
About a year ago, in June 2025, I had a long discussion with Anonymous for the Voiceless (AV) founder Paul Bashir, on David Ramms’ YouTube channel. In spite of our different views on animal advocacy, we kept it civil and in the end made each other a promise: Paul would read my book, I would participate in a cube.

A few weeks ago, I honored my part of the deal. In July 2026, participated in Anonymous activism in Amsterdam, outreaching on two consecutive days, for about six hours in total. David and Anni Ramms filmed the whole thing, and he’ll moderate and record the follow-up discussion at Vegan Campout in August. I’m sharing my preliminary experiences and opinions here.

For those not familiar with Anonymous’ approach: a few (masked) people show screens with footage of how humans abuse animals, on some busy square or street. Other activists approach those who seem to engage with the footage. They will try to have a conversation, following a “protocol”: a list of questions that hopefully ends with people committing to stop exploiting animals and going vegan. Or better yet (the ultimate goal): becoming a vegan activist. The questions are entirely focused on the ethical aspect of exploiting animals (I’ll get back to that).

This is a bit of a long posts. There’s a summary at the very end.

Respect and criticism

I have some critical thoughts, after my experience, but it’s important to note that these are expressed with a lot of respect for what the Anonymous people are doing. I have only admiration for people who commit to helping make things better for animals, in whatever way, shape, or form, and spend a significant amount of time doing it. It was clear to me how seriously all of the activists were taking their job, and how committed they were.

I’m sure most of those who knew me knew that I was to some extent critical of their approach. Nevertheless, I felt very welcome and appreciated. I went in with an open mind, and applied the approach as faithfully as I could (even though I experimented a bit now and then).

I also need to note that obviously my experience was limited. Other people have done this much longer than I have. Also, how this particular group of activists comported themselves is probably not entirely representative of all AV groups. Still, the outreach is pretty streamlined, and as Paul Bashir was there himself, one may assume that this was the most “orthodox” execution of the approach.

In spite of the critical comments below, I find that there’s a lot to like about Anonymous for the Voiceless, and I think it’s great that they’re around. It is a scalable model for individual outreach, and many people can (after a minimal amount of training) participate in it and help advance things for animals.

I do believe a certain (limited) number of people can be reached in this way, and that we can get new activists out of this, who may go on to stay in the movement for a long time and do great things. Chances of success are higher because activists try to focus on the people who seem open, and quickly let go (after three “strikes”) of those who (in activists’ eyes) are not ready.

I’m thankful for this experience and to Paul, my buddy, and the other activists welcoming me. I enjoyed it a lot. I am usually not confrontational when I talk to people, but it felt good to be like that for a bit, and see where it took me. I guess that now and then, “holding people accountable” can be a good strategy. I’m sure I will apply some of the approach in certain circumstances.

My experience

I was assigned a buddy, who I first shadowed, after which he shadowed me. We could hear each other’s conversations through a microphone attached to our shirts. My buddy’s comments on my outreach were instructive, and helped me stick to the protocol - which I was there to test. The protocol starts with “Hello, how do you feel about humans exploiting animals?” and then ideally goes on for about eight more questions.

Maybe my very first experience was beginner’s luck (even if I had to speak French, which is not my forte). I bumped into a couple and their young son, who were very open to answering my questions, and very concerned about animals. First the woman and then the son agreed there was nothing keeping them from being vegan, and they promised they would be from now on. The man seemed reluctant, but - improvising a little bit - I told him it would be hard for his wife and son if he didn’t go along, and he agreed as well.

The commitment to go vegan is what the AV activists are after. Once they have that, they get people to confirm that animals deserve to have people speak out for them, and even ask them to stand with a screen for at least a few minutes and be an activist for animals.

Out of maybe 20 conversations, I got to the yes-I’ll-stop-exploiting-animals point only one other time. I heard from other people it was a slow day (sometimes it seemed there were more activists than people stopping to watch the footage).

Pragmatism and idealism

In my book and work, I make a distinction between pragmatic and idealistic activism. These are not super-defined terms, but one way to make this distinction is to say that pragmatic activism is more outcome-focused (results are most important) while one of the characteristics of idealistic activism is that it focuses heavily on following certain rules.

I’m sure Anonymous activists will think of their activism as very much outcome-focused. However, while - as stated - their commitment to impact is clear, following rules seems also quite important to them. Every time after a chat, my buddy would tell me the terms and expressions I had used but shouldn’t have. It all came down to making sure people understand the problem of animal exploitation as a whole, rather than focus on subparts (e.g. meat) or distractions (e.g. diet).

This focus on exploitation as the problem means that talking about anything other than general animal exploitation seems problematic. It’s not really done to talk about suffering, circumstances, or specific practices. Or if one does, it has to be in a way that connects these aspects - again - to the general problem of animal exploitation. Also: don’t talk about animal products, neither in the abstract, nor concretely about milk, meat, leather… Rather talk about body secretions, body parts, animal skin. Sometimes I felt the “correct” terms were not the ones that were most easily understandable for the audience.

Flexibility vs. rigidity

This is part of a wider issue that I see, which is that the outreacher should not adapt the protocol to whoever they have in front of them. There’s no meeting people where they are, there’s only the question of whether they are ready for the protocol or not.

The clearest example I saw of that was when an outreacher talked to a woman who said she was vegan already. After a few questions, it became clear she was plant-based (e.g. not avoiding leather etc.) and the outreacher continued with the protocol, as if she was nowhere near vegan - while I felt she was very close. The woman received zero recognition for where she was already, and the conversation did not feel productive at all to me. I told the outreacher my honest opinion: that this had been worse than nothing.

Here’s an example that I find even more problematic (I didn’t witness it). The person in this video has been an ethical vegan for twenty years. Paul Bashir himself talks to him, but the poor man doesn’t get any pat on the back. On the contrary, because this man is not actively doing outreach and believes people should make their own choices, Paul ends the conversation calling him a disgusting human being. The fact that this video is posted online seems to mean that the AV people are okay with its content? If I had to score to the AV approach, then from whatever number I rate it out of ten, I probably would subtract three or four points for this alone.

The activists seemed not to mind leaving people with a “bad” feeling, for instance by walking out of the conversation, or even being very confrontational (or quite rude) to people. They believe this will make people think. I’m not saying it’s impossible that this happens, but it doesn’t seem very likely (something to test - see below).

A rule I found hard to follow was not to shake a person’s hand after what I thought was a nice interaction. Even if they stuck out their hand, my buddy told me, we refuse it because the victims would not like to see us shake their oppressor’s hand. I can understand the rationale, but it didn’t feel helpful to me to refuse a hand after a person seemed to appreciate the conversation.

Optimizing for the handshake

In this particular type of outreach, all the attention seems to be directed at getting a person to commit to no longer exploiting animals. I agree that’s a nice goal, but I felt this focus was often at the cost of appreciating and getting the most out of the conversation (the process) itself.

To some extent the activists seem to look at the conversations as black or white: committing to go vegan: good, not getting there: failure. Personally I felt I had some great conversations where I felt I was sowing seeds, but where (understandably) the person was not ready to commit on the spot.

Conversely, I’m not so sure about the people committing. In a meeting, we analyzed interactions on video (many convos are recorded to spread on social media and to learn from). Showing a successful interaction (ending in a handshake), the activist asked what we thought.

I didn’t want to be a downer, but said I gave it at most a 20% chance that the person was now vegan. The others seemed surprised at this. I explained that the conversation was just one moment in a person’s life. While I had no doubt that he was now closer than before, the man would be stepping into the real world, be confronted, perhaps, by a spouse or children who hadn’t been in the conversation, would see meat on every corner of every street, etc. It’s hard to believe one conversation and one “pledge” are strong enough to counter the forces of gravity and inertia. (And if it was enough, it probably means that the person was very close already even before the conversation?)

I guess I’m most critical of how much confidence AV has in the effectiveness of moral suasion, and a particularly strict approach to it to boot. People don’t take the step from a conversation to conviction to permanent behavior change easily.

Controlling the conversation

I like that activists are told to keep control of the conversation (with the help of the protocol). It’s too easy to get sidetracked by all kinds of objections from their interlocutors, which would prevent the activist from making their essential points. However, there seem to be downsides to this. For one thing, activists will focus on getting through their questions. I heard one member of the public say to the activist: “You are working with a script. We are not having a conversation: this is me answering your questions.”

The other downside is that sincerely meant questions and objections are often not taken seriously enough or not responded to. When people express health concerns, these are not addressed. When they say they agree but it’s hard, they get no acknowledgment. When they say they’ve already gone part of the way they don’t get - like I stated before - any recognition. And when people ask: okay, but how? activists are not supposed to give them any pointers, except to say that they can find that out for themselves. Which is true but not necessarily helpful.

AV firmly believes that the WHY comes first. Once you are convinced, you can overcome all obstacles. I believe that the HOW being difficult is in itself an obstacle to understanding the WHY. Once people see that there are tasty, affordable products available, their defensiveness against listening to the WHY can be lowered. Sure, it won’t hurt if they understand the principle of veganism, but understanding it and putting it into practice has huge repercussions.

Other asks?

When people aren’t ready to commit to going vegan, the AV activist is not supposed to present them with another option, nor are they supposed to applaud any other commitment the person makes (like “I’ll look into it; I’ll try it for a week; I’ll think about it…”). I suspect this is because anything less than the commitment to go vegan is unethical, either to do or to suggest. Again, rules.

Personally, I would present people with other options. Even getting them to commit that this month, this week, or even just tomorrow, they wouldn’t use animal products, or that just their next meal would be vegan, would in my eyes be a win. I especially believe that when people DO something, this can have an impact on their commitment and beliefs - which is why I think their grabbing a screen and standing in the cube for a few minutes can be quite meaningful. I think the focus on this is great. But why not also have them do smaller things? Give people, for instance, a discount code from a collaborating restaurant in the area, and measure how many people use it.

Does it work?

Which brings me to impact measurement. How well does the approach work? AV talks about thousands of people going vegan and/or becoming animal activists in the course of a one-month demonstration (e.g. 7,000 people during the action in Cologne, DE). I’m skeptical, but could we come to a trustworthy answer if we do better than just taking people at their word?

Paul Bashir’s answer to people who tell him to measure more is that it’s impossible to be sure, unless we hire private detectives. I think that’s not a satisfactory answer. I can see how a follow-up could be helpful. I asked some of the activists why they don’t routinely ask - after successful interactions - for people’s email address or phone number, and follow up a month and/or three months later, to see how it’s going. There were some logistical objections, but I got no clear answer why this wouldn’t be done. Even if it was consistently done for only a limited amount of time (say two months), this could yield some good data to extrapolate from.

Measuring people’s post-interaction response seems especially important when making big claims that run against our intuitions or against what we know from research. The question of whether letting people walk off with a bad feeling about themselves is productive or not seems to be a good candidate for research. As is the question of whether a committed person really follows through or not.

Paul Bashir claims AV’s method is the most effective outreach method in the movement. I do not underestimate the value of him interacting with thousands of people, but this does not seem to be a claim one can make on the basis of just one’s own (or one’s group’s) experience.

In any case, other people who are more research-experienced than I am could chip in on this.

Looking ahead

There’s more to tell, no doubt. I look forward to exploring the pros and cons of the Anonymous approach further with Paul, and I wish AV all the best. I might participate again in the future.

I encourage vegans who are not active to join a group and try out the approach (find your local chapter here). Apart from the real-world impact you may have with it, AV also offers a community. Dog knows how hard it can be to be a vegan in this world. Communities help.

Below is a summary.

Subscribe for more posts that confront, comfort or inspire.

What I like:


● the focus on the people presumed to be open/ready
● the guidance activists get (from the protocol and from each other)
● activists constantly learning and being open to feedback
● activists taking control of the conversation (though at some cost)
● the focus on developping activists
● the low threshold for participation
● the community

What would make the approach better still (IMHO)

● not just optimizing for handshakes but valuing the process as well
● having something else to ask than go vegan
● being warmer and more connecting (guilt is usually not productive); absolutely avoid rudeness
● being less focused on rules, terms, language and being entirely correct
● improving the installation (more, bigger and sharper screens)
● measuring more
● respecting what people already do, acknowlediging sincerely felt objections

item.title: The vegan trap
item.description: Are we making animal advocacy harder than it needs to be?
item.content:encoded:
As a vegan for almost thirty years, I’ve long had second thoughts about how effective veganism is for helping animals. I am not alone in this. Recently others have expressed doubts about veganism (see for instance here, here, here, here, or here)

To be sure, veganism has its uses. In essence, veganism is about boycotting animal products - which are almost invariably the products of suffering and exploitation. The hope is that with enough people participating in this boycott, we’ll have an impact on demand, and fewer - ultimately no - animals would be used for food (or other purposes). Veganism also has a signalling function: we show that we don’t participate in animal cruelty because we think it’s wrong. And veganism provides our movement with an identity, which can help with internal cohesion. When a vegan meets another vegan, they know that they “get it”. No conversation is necessary. They have arrived at the same place as we have. They’re one of us. We understand each other. And we’ll feel betrayed and take it personally when others give up on veganism.

Vegans, no doubt, deserve respect. It’s not easy to be vegan in this world and it requires commitment. I have the utmost respect for vegans and still generally consider them “my people”. And no worries, I’m continuing to be vegan, and so should you.

The number of vegans is hardly growing.

But veganism also has quite a few disadvantages and challenges. Before I get into these, let me add that in the thirty years I’ve been into animal activism, I’ve gotten a lot of criticism from vegans, because I’ve always criticized vegan policing and purity politics. I think those are not useful (see below). To say this is to invite scapegoating, bullying and gatekeeping upon oneself - and sometimes all of this can get quite nasty (here’s an example of a person who’s been disingenuously attacking me for many years). It doesn’t bode well for our movement that people who have worked for the animals for decades still have to explain their intentions.

Subscribe to read more posts that comfort, confront or inspire

Over the years, I’ve often heard this elegant-sounding theory of change: if every vegan made one other person vegan in one year and those new vegans would do the same, then in five or six years a country could be vegan, starting from a very small base of 1%. It sounds feasible. It’s actually hard to think of why it would not work. But of course it doesn’t. The number of vegans is not increasing. And it’s not just being vegan that’s hard. Staying vegan is also hard. Surveys show that at any given moment there are more ex-vegans than vegans.

Many organizations have therefore moved on from personal vegan outreach to institutional change, welfare reforms, reduction asks, and climate and health messaging. Still, veganism is very much a part of our DNA as a movement. Which is why I’m addressing it.

Veganism has many challenges and downsides

  • It can become a very strong in-group identity, which, like I said, is an advantage to a point, but it means that it becomes harder for other people to join us.

  • Veganism may become the price of entry to our “club”. If somebody’s not vegan, some animal activists may wonder if they belong among us. This dynamic makes us quite unique as a movement, and I can’t think of similar dynamics in other movements. Imagine the environmental movement: you won’t be shown the door if you show up at a protest with a petrol car. Few other movements have strict requirements and black-and-white rules like the animal rights movement often has.

  • Veganism may imply an over-focus on individual change and personal responsibility at the cost of activism or political engagement. Maybe you heard that the concept of the personal carbon footprint was developed by an advertising agency, Ogilvy, for British Petroleum. The idea was to show people what they were personally responsible for in terms of climate impact, and thus take some of the focus and blame away from the fossil fuel companies.

  • Veganism can also be a hindrance to collaboration. I remember, in my time when I was working in an organization, how now and then we said no to certain opportunities where we could amplify our message. Some party with a broad reach would want to create and spread a recipe booklet with us, but they wanted some non-vegan recipes in it. So we said no - a missed opportunity based on principles.

  • Veganism can become an end in itself, the only thing that matters. And being vegan may give one a moral licence not to do more. One may think: I’m vegan, I’m doing my part.

  • Veganism may push us to communicate ineffectively: a representative of an animal organization, speaking in public, may know that pragmatically it’s better to be more moderate, but may fear the backlash from vegans - and thus say things that are not optimal for the public at large.

  • Finally, veganism is a very demanding and unattractive concept, and if we’re asking people to go vegan, we’re putting the bar very high. Veganism seems daunting and difficult, and people doubt that it’s healthy. People dislike vegans. And once you’re vegan it may be hard to keep up because of health, social and other challenges, compassion fatigue, and so on.

Creating barriers

One of the main problems I see is that if someone is vegan, this makes that person automatically seem quite different from non-vegans, as if we’re talking about different kinds of people, with different identities. Veganism, in this sense, draws up a wall and makes it harder to speak with others.

The basic dynamic at work is what we call do-gooder derogation. When somebody does something good, it often makes another person feel bad about themselves because the other is not doing that good thing. I’ve written in another post about Anthony Robbins saying that our universal fear is to not be enough, to not be good or smart enough. Vegans, by being vegan, unintentionally tell other people who are not vegan that they’re not good enough. That, at least, is how it’s often perceived, and that is what creates a wall and stops conversation and relationships. Do-gooder derogation means that the non-vegan is going to derogate the vegan (the do-gooder). They’re going to attack and ridicule them out of self-defense, and the chances that the non-vegan will change their behaviour get smaller.

What if we had never invented veganism?

This is a question I’ve started to ask myself over the last few years. What if Donald Watson had never come up with the concept in 1944? It seems absurd to want to help animals, farmed animals in particular, and all the while not completely avoiding their consumption.

It’s not a perfect comparison but the anti-slavery abolitionists had a concept very similar to veganism: the so-called Free Produce Movement. Its adherents were people who boycotted any products from slavery (such as sugar, tobacco or cotton). They even had their own stores, similar to vegan stores. This concept, however, was discussed and criticized a lot and, after some time, was let go of. It was never a major thing in the abolitionist movement. Abolitionists thought the bar was too high and instead focused on political, societal, and institutional change rather than individual purity and individual ethical behaviour.

Then what do we do?

First: let go of the insistence on purity - at least by other people. Be as pure as you want, but don’t put the bar too high for others. The requirement to be vegan always, everywhere, in every situation is ineffective because it turns people off. It’s also impossible, because there are all kinds of animal ingredients in our food, in our life, in our practices. It can be unnecessary - for instance, if now and then one eats animal products from a dumpster, one has no impact on demand. Finally, it’s insufficient, because vegan products might still be detrimental for animals, the planet or other people.

I’d say we’d be more successful if we saw veganism as a 98% thing rather than a 100% thing. Melanie Joy talks about being “as vegan as possible.” Veganish is another term we could use. Again, do what you want, just don’t expect purity from others, and certainly don’t exclude them if their definition of veganism is not sufficiently close to yours. You’ll only make the vegan club smaller.

Secondly, we can use other asks. We can talk about reduction, about vegetarianism. We can launch concepts like “home veganism” (eating vegan at home, not so strict outside) or “weekday veganism”. There are different ways to make it easier to get people to take the first step.

Thirdly, rather than focus on personal diet change, we should go more institutional, structural, political. Rather than asking lifestyle changes from people, we can ask them to help us campaign, vote, donate and thus contribute to systemic change. Chris Bryant from Bryant Research talks about Vegan 2.0, where veganism is about avoiding the most horrible forms of animal suffering and being active against them.

This is actually reflected in the original rules of the Vegan Society. Back in 1944 they set up an associate, so a member, who “makes no promise as to behaviour, but declares himself in agreement with the object”.

The vegan trap

Suppose I was able to prove to you (obviously I am not), without a shadow of a doubt, that our use of the concept of veganism is detrimental for animals. Would we change?

I don’t think so - because vegans are in what I call the vegan trap. We are, I think, to some extent the hostages of our ideals and of our movement. They make us do or avoid things out of principle, out of good intentions - and this is not always the best thing for animals.

The way we are trapped is that we cannot easily change ourselves. We cannot choose not to be vegan, even for a moment, even if it would be pragmatic to do so. We can’t stop believing that moral persuasion works - even if we see that veganism still hasn’t made a dent in animal products consumption. Veganism is also part of who we are, part of our identity. We can’t shake it. And we are very uncomfortable with inconsistencies: it doesn’t feel good to make exceptions. We want to do the 100%.

Many of us also have a hard time stopping trying to influence others from going vegan. Imagine a non-vegan turns up at a vegan potluck. What do vegans do? They zoom in on their new “target” and will try to convert them, for better or for worse. Because it’s what we believe in.

Lastly, part of the vegan trap is also the group pressure. Even if we think it might be wiser to do or say this or that, the rest of the group might push us back in line.

We need more non-vegans

Often, vegans’ attitudes toward vegans and non-vegans come down to something like this: a vegan can do nothing wrong; a non-vegan can do nothing right. We don’t criticize the vegan who never leaves his house and doesn’t do any influencing. We do criticize a non-vegan advocate for animals.

Vegans are one percent of the population. It will be difficult, if not impossible, to change things for animals with this small group alone. Fortunately, there are many more people who can theoretically help animals - including farmed animals - than there are vegans. There are many more people who are in favour of the closing of slaughterhouses than there are vegans. There are many people who are not vegan but have money to help animals. Take Dustin Moskovitz, a co-founder of Facebook. With his fund, Coefficient Giving, he’s the biggest funder of animal welfare in the world. But he’s not vegan.

This is not all. Non-vegans may be better advocates sometimes. They’re less limited by our rules - they’re not in the vegan trap. They can speak more freely. We are often beholden to our orthodoxy and cannot always bring the best and most suitable message. They are often less threatening and more relatable, so they might be better messengers for animals.

A simple point about communication: it consists of what is said, how it is said, and who says it. Who is the messenger? Who is talking to whom? We know from research, at least from this one study, that messages by non-vegans about the same thing are perceived as less threatening than messages by vegans. Non-vegans can be better spokespeople for our cause, sometimes.

Here’s an example. Days Without Meat (Dagen Zonder Vlees) was an extremely successful vegetarian campaign in Belgium, asking people to go vegetarian or reduce meat consumption during the period of Lent (the 40 days before Easter). At some point over 100,000 people actively participated, in a small country like Belgium, and everyone knew about it. This campaign was organized by a female student who was not vegan or even vegetarian. But I think the effect was that the people who participated didn’t have the impression that there was some vegan from on high telling others what to do. Instead, the audience was in the same boat as the campaigners, meaning they felt a lot less judged. (Note: in a newspaper interview, this young woman said she never said no to a good chicken curry. The fact that I cursed inwardly when I read that, shows that I, too, am in the vegan trap).

Enlisting non-vegans’ help for animals

How do we reach these non-vegans and get them to help animals? We need to do at least three things.

  1. We need to attract them. Show them that they are capable of helping, even if they’re not vegan. One example comes from Aaron Boddy, from Ambitious Impact. He is very committed to animals, but posted this on his LinkedIn: “I ran an animal charity and I eat dairy.” Some people objected, but I think it’s definitely worth trying to avoid people thinking that they can’t participate because they’re not vegan.

  2. We need to allow them to be among us. Here is a little thought experiment. Imagine a vegan pride parade. Who is welcome to be there? Are non-vegans welcome? I don’t think that at the moment they are as welcome as straight people are at a Pride parade, but they definitely should be.

  3. We need to keep them, and with this, I think I mean: “keep them non-vegan”. Often when some vegans will make the case for including non-vegans, they’ll say that these people will turn vegan anyway by being among us. That may be true in many cases, but I’m not sure if it’s actually the best outcome. Maybe some non-vegans should STAY non-vegan - at least for quite some time - to help increase the heterogeneity of our group, so that we can attract more people still. If every non-vegan joining goes vegan tomorrow, we won’t have increased our recruiting power.

All of the above are things for your consideration, and I’m 100% sure of exactly none of it. These are ideas that go against the vegan grain, but I believe as people who take up the plight of beings who can’t fight for themselves, that we keep asking hard questions - and still trust each other to have the best of intentions.

Thanks for reading.

item.title: To breed or not to breed
item.description: Should animal people have children?
item.content:encoded:
My girlfriend and I got together about 17 years ago. Our very fresh relationship seemed doomed when we found out about our different feelings on having children: she wanted them, I didn’t. I suggested we’d evaluate after one year together, and see where we’d stand then. As it happened, after that period was over, my girlfriend concluded she didn’t want children after all. We ended up with dogs, cats, chickens, pigs, ducks and turkeys instead. For now, I never regretted not having children (I’m 53).

I find the should-you-have-children question always a good conversation topic - particularly in a context of people who want to make the world a better place. Below is my current thinking on the psychological, philosophical, social and economic aspects of this life choice.

Psychology: are we happier with children?

Humans may be evolutionarily wired such that their most meaningful and pleasurable experiences are tied to procreation. I have no doubt that having children can bring a lot of happiness to one’s life - and to the lives of grandparents, siblings, and other people who get to connect with the person in question.

Apart from a sense of happiness, children can also give people a sense of meaning and purpose. However, it seems that in the case of activists/changemakers - which I’m primarily concerned with here - that meaning and purpose will often be present already. For them a child might provide a smaller additional value than for the average person. Also, having a sense of meaning is not the same as something actually being meaningful in an objective sense.

The research on happiness and having (no) children gives a mixed picture. According to a US study, parents experienced both more positive and negative emotions; a British-German study found happiness rose after a first child, but returned to a baseline after that. Of course how happy one is with a child will depend on many things: on how happy and healthy the child itself is, on the relationship between the parents (if both are present at all), childcare support, general life satisfaction, and so on. It can also depend on to what degree one wanted the child. We shouldn’t underestimate the pressure on some people to have children (on women in particular, in certain cultures more so than others). Having them when you didn’t want them doesn’t seem good (conversely, denying yourself children for e.g. ecological reasons while you do want them, would also not be good, at least for oneself - see this piece by Julia Wise).

Social: how does (not) having children impact our impact on the world?

Children seem like a massive opportunity cost for people trying to make the world a better place. Raising a child takes thousands of hours and a lot of money, some of which could otherwise go towards advocacy, donations or helping others (who were in the world anyway) directly. An activist could plausibly persuade several existing people to care (no matter how hard that is) in far less time than it takes to raise one child.

Obviously, there’s a good chance that - through genetics or upbringing - the children of caring and committed people may themselves turn out to be caring and committed to improving the world. If this effect is strong, it would be bad if such people didn’t have (many) children, and leave the breeding, so to speak, to the indifferent. In this context, the movie ***Idiocracy*** is often mentioned. It imagines a future society that is less intelligent because only the less intelligent people have been procreating.

I’m not sure how strong a “survival of the less caring” argument is and how well it applies to veganism/caring about animals. Ideological groups probably grow more through conversion than through birth - though the latter can be the case for groups with high fertility and closed communities.

We also have to ask how big the influence of parents on their children is, either via the genes or upbringing. There seems to be no or very little data available regarding animals or veganism, so we have to go a bit broader. Genes account for significant differences in empathy: twin-study estimates put heritability at about 48% for emotional empathy and 27% for cognitive empathy (these are population-level estimates, not percentages “passed on” to a child).¹

Upbringing can obviously shape values as well. This effect seems strongest in the case of religion (and politics to a lesser degree), and when the child is raised within a broader ecosystem of “believers”.² The latter is usually not the case with veganism or animal activism: children mostly grow up in a non-vegan environment. Overall, it seems that parents can pass on a disposition to care and engage, but I’m not sure if this is a good argument from an activist standpoint (and we should be wary of expecting too much from our children anyway - not only because we might be in for a major disappointment).

Even if there’s a good chance that one’s child will become an animal advocate, the opportunity cost point still holds. There are plenty of people with children who still find the time to do big things in the world, but for the typical person, having a child will mean a significant reduction of capacity. As with personal happiness, this will depend on many factors, including the investment of the spouse (or grandparents) in the household.

What irks me sometimes (and I shouldn’t be judgmental but I can’t always help it) is how the world of new parents often seems to shrink and they get much more parochial, focusing on the family and the wellbeing of the child - which could e.g. make them buy a big, safe car they otherwise wouldn’t have bought. I’ve also heard enough stories of parents falling off the vegan wagon after having a child.

Again this seems to cut both ways: some parents claim their empathy for the world was awakened or deepened through having a child - maybe similar to the way many people start caring about animals in general after taking in a dog or a cat.

Philosophy: does it matter for a human to be born? Or how many people there are?

Parents and other humans can be (positively or negatively) impacted by the arrival of a new human in the world. But is the existence of the new human important for that human himself/herself? In other words, is it important for a human to be born?

This question brings us into the thorny thickets of the domain within philosophy called population ethics, which is about evaluating different possible populations, and problems like whether bringing new people into existence is good, bad, or morally neutral. There are many questions in population ethics, but few have solid answers.

For me it’s obvious that we don’t harm someone by NOT bringing them into the world, even if they would have led the most blissful life. I’m assuming here there is nothing before birth: no waiting room in which a soul waits to be born, bored or scared out of its wits. So anyone deciding not to have a child is not harming that would-be being, because, simply put, there IS no one to be harmed. Note that vegans give a similar answer to meat eaters who claim that if people didn’t eat meat, billions of animals would not be born (sometimes called the “logic of the larder” argument). We tell this meat eater that farmed animals’ lives are generally horrible: it’s preferable to not be born. Not being born is not bad, while creating a bad life is bad.³ This is also why adopting a human who is already in the world and needs help, seems quite good.

Personally**, I’m indifferent about bringing even the happiest being into the world** (setting aside the impact they will have on the parents or the world at large). Like I said, it’s a thorny topic that I’ll keep for another time.

Antinatalism

By now I may sound like an antinatalist, who believes that bringing someone into the world is always wrong, because every life contains some suffering, and no one can consent to the risk of being born. I sympathize, but I wouldn’t call myself an antinatalist, for various reasons. One of them is that antinatalism, when consistently followed, would lead to human extinction. Some vegans and environmentalists may believe this would be a good thing. I try to remain optimistic about humanity and hope that down the road, if we clean up our act and become wiser and more technologically mature, we might be able to help animals who are suffering in the wild. And what if one day we discover other planets in our or other galaxies where we know there’s a lot of suffering, and could help? It would be bad then if we didn’t exist. (Oops, the initial to-breed-or-not-to-breed question has brought us to other planets, it seems. More of what I wrote on this here)

Another problem with antinatalism is that at least in my experience there’s a significant overlap with misanthropy, which in the animal movement is a bit of a thing. Given what humans do to other animals, I can totally understand misanthropy, but it doesn’t seem very strategic, in that it’s alienating. A largely misanthropic movement will have a hard time attracting new people.

Economy: do we need many people?

Finally, there’s the question of whether a healthy economy requires a large/growing population. Young people pay for older people’s pensions and healthcare, so having children can benefit public finances⁵. Against this, we can say that a better economy doesn’t automatically mean happier lives. According to a study covering 40 countries, moderately low fertility can support material wellbeing, while very low fertility does create problems. In the long term, a shrinking population might produce fewer researchers and ideas, stalling growth and innovation.⁴ But there are other factors involved (like the quality, as opposed to the quantity, of the population), or where exactly we’ll go with AI (or where AI takes us).

Child-free people sometimes complain about paying taxes for schools, childcare and other services they don’t use. But the argument cuts both ways: other people’s children will help fund the pensions and healthcare of the child-free, and may one day care for them. Parents bear much of the cost of raising those future adults, while the benefits are shared more widely. In that sense, there’s something to the argument that the child-free are free-riders. Of course, raising children is only one way of contributing to our collective future. What we do with the time and money we don’t spend on children matters too.

In conclusion: rational arguments and emotions

Many of the above reasons for and against having children could be used to construct some kind of altruistic argument for one’s choice. However, for the majority of people, the choice to have children or not is probably mostly intuitive/emotional. I used to argue, from a relatively young age, that having children wasn’t a good idea, but to be honest my reasons were probably rationalizations of what I felt intuitively. I never felt any desire to have children. I never walk up to someone’s baby the way I’ll cross the street to see a puppy (or any dog).

I’m also aware that my rather negative feelings about people having children often have pretty mundane grounds. I don’t like how loud children can be, for instance (I think I suffer from misophonia). And whenever friends announce they are pregnant, I’m always a bit despairing about the friendship, because in many cases I won’t see much of them in the future. I understand they have other priorities and less time after having children, but also, part of it may lie with me: I really dislike catching up with friends when one or more of their children are present. They make good conversations pretty much impossible. Dogs don’t pose that problem.

To conclude, a few things I feel moderately strongly about:

  • There’s no real strong argument either way. We may lose some good activists to having children, but it’s definitely possible to combine children and activism, and having children can have good effects for the world.

  • Negative attitudes towards humans and humanity - whether they be anti-children, antinatalist, or misanthropic - do not benefit our movement.6 Social norms against having children might be alienating.

  • I prefer humanity to continue, mainly because if it grows up, it can help other creatures.

  • There is more financial room for doing good without having children. And when a child-free couple dies, all the money they have left is free to go to charity.

  • It may not be feasible for everyone or desireable for anyone with a wish for their own child, but adoption seems like a great option.

Any arguments I’ve skipped? I’m interested to hear your thoughts.

For more posts that comfort, confront or inspire, subscribe to The Vegan Strategist.

Notes

I used AI to help me with references.

¹ Abramson, L., Uzefovsky, F., Toccaceli, V. & Knafo-Noam, A. (2020). The genetic and environmental origins of emotional and cognitive empathy: Review and meta-analyses of twin studies. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 114, 113-133. Link

² Jennings, M. K., Stoker, L. & Bowers, J. (2009). Politics across generations: Family transmission reexamined. The Journal of Politics, 71(3), 782-799. Link

³ But what if animals’ lives were wonderful (before being killed for consumption)? Would that change things? Or is it better never to bring a being into existence, however wonderful their life might be, simply because someone will eventually end it? Again, for another time.

⁴ Jones, C. I. (2022). The end of economic growth? Unintended consequences of a declining population. American Economic Review, 112(11), 3489-3527. Link

⁵ Wolf, Lee, Miller et al. (2011). Link

6 Note that I’m mainly talking about standard (colloquial) misanthropy. Philosophical misanthropy is something else: it’s a reasoned verdict that humanity as a collective has failed morally. A philosophical misanthrope does not necessarily hate people, nor do they have to deny human goodness or reject personal relationships.
